subject: ela
intro: Each problem gives you a short informational passage and a non-text format (a table, chart, timeline, map, or diagram described in words). Read both carefully. To answer, you must combine what the words say with what the format shows. Choosing only from the text, or only from the format, will not give the full answer.

items.prompt:
Passage: Maple Town built a new bus line in 2010 to connect its growing neighborhoods. City leaders said the bus line was meant to ease traffic during the morning rush. At first, only a few hundred people rode each day. Reports later claimed that ridership 'climbed steadily' once people learned the routes. By the middle of the decade, the buses were often full. Officials pointed to the rising numbers as proof that the line was worth its cost. They argued the trend would continue for years.

Table 1: Average daily riders on the Maple Town bus line
Year 2010: 400 riders
Year 2012: 1,100 riders
Year 2014: 2,300 riders
Year 2016: 3,800 riders
Year 2018: 5,200 riders

Using both the passage and Table 1, which row best supports the passage's statement that ridership 'climbed steadily' once people learned the routes? Explain how the data confirms the words.
items.answer: Every later row in Table 1 supports the claim because each year shown has more riders than the year before (400, then 1,100, then 2,300, then 3,800, then 5,200). The 2018 row (5,200 riders) shows the highest total and best demonstrates the steady climb described in the words, since it caps a pattern where the number rises at every step.

steps: The words make a claim about a trend: ridership 'climbed steadily' over time.
The table supplies the actual numbers the words leave out, so I must read the rows to test the claim.
Check each step: 400 to 1,100 to 2,300 to 3,800 to 5,200. Every value is larger than the one before it, with no drops.
Combine the two sources: the words say 'climbed steadily' and the rising rows confirm it, with 2018 (5,200) showing the climb reaching its highest point.
I cannot answer from the words alone, because they never give a number, and I cannot answer from one row alone, because the claim is about a pattern across years.

items.prompt:
Passage: The Arctic fox changes color with the seasons. In winter its fur is thick and white, which helps it blend into the snow. As spring arrives and the snow melts, the fur turns brown or gray to match the rocky ground. Scientists studied one fox population for several years. They reported that the foxes 'turned white earlier than usual' during one cold year when snow came early. The report did not say exactly which month.

Chart 1: Month when foxes' fur first turned white, by year
Year 1: November
Year 2: November
Year 3: October
Year 4: November
Year 5: November

Using both the passage and Chart 1, which year was the cold year when the foxes 'turned white earlier than usual'? Explain how you know.
items.answer: Year 3 was the cold year. The chart shows the fur usually first turned white in November, but in Year 3 it turned white in October, which is earlier than the other years. The passage's phrase 'turned white earlier than usual' matches the one October entry in the chart.

steps: The words say the foxes 'turned white earlier than usual' in one cold year but never name the year.
The chart gives the month for each year, which is the detail the words leave out.
Find the usual month: four of the five years show November, so November is 'usual.'
Find the exception: Year 3 shows October, which comes before November, so it is 'earlier than usual.'
Combine: the words describe an earlier-than-normal change, and the chart points to Year 3 as the only year that fits, so Year 3 is the cold year.

items.prompt:
Passage: A glacier named Long River Ice has been shrinking for decades. Visitors who return each summer say the ice looks 'noticeably shorter,' but the passage never states how much it has retreated. Park scientists measure the glacier's length from a fixed marker each year. They warn that if the loss continues, a popular hiking trail near the glacier's edge may have to move. The passage says the change has been 'dramatic' but gives no figures.

Table 1: Length of Long River Ice from the fixed marker
Year 2000: 4,200 meters
Year 2005: 3,900 meters
Year 2010: 3,500 meters
Year 2015: 2,950 meters
Year 2020: 2,300 meters

Using both the passage and Table 1, by how many meters did the glacier shrink from 2000 to 2020, and how does this number support the word 'dramatic'?
items.answer: The glacier shrank by 1,900 meters (4,200 minus 2,300). This large drop of nearly half its starting length supports the passage's word 'dramatic,' because the table supplies the exact size of the loss that the words only described in general terms.

steps: The words call the change 'dramatic' but give no number, so the size of the loss must come from the table.
Find the starting length in 2000: 4,200 meters.
Find the ending length in 2020: 2,300 meters.
Subtract to get the loss: 4,200 minus 2,300 equals 1,900 meters.
Combine the sources: the table's 1,900 meter loss is a large amount (close to half the original length), which gives concrete support to the passage's word 'dramatic.'

items.prompt:
Passage: Honeybees tell each other where to find flowers by performing a 'waggle dance' inside the hive. A bee that has found food runs in a straight line while shaking its body, then circles back to repeat the run. Scientists explain that the angle of the straight run, measured from straight up, matches the angle of the flowers measured from the direction of the sun. The passage says the dance 'points the way' but does not explain how an angle becomes a direction.

Diagram 1: The waggle dance angle
Top of the honeycomb stands for the direction of the sun.
A waggle run tilted 40 degrees to the right of straight up means: fly toward the food at 40 degrees to the right of the sun.
A waggle run pointed straight up means: fly directly toward the sun.
A waggle run pointed straight down means: fly directly away from the sun.

Using both the passage and Diagram 1, explain how the diagram helps a reader understand the passage's statement that the dance 'points the way.'
items.answer: The diagram shows that the tilt of the bee's straight run stands for a direction relative to the sun, so a run tilted 40 degrees right means fly 40 degrees right of the sun, straight up means toward the sun, and straight down means away from it. This makes the passage's vague phrase 'points the way' concrete by explaining that the angle of the dance is the actual direction to the food.

steps: The words say the dance 'points the way' but do not explain how, leaving the method unclear.
The diagram supplies the missing rule: the top of the comb equals the sun, and the tilt of the run equals an angle measured from the sun.
Read the labeled cases: straight up means toward the sun, 40 degrees right means 40 degrees right of the sun, straight down means away from the sun.
Combine: the diagram turns the abstract idea in the words into a clear system, showing that the angle of the dance is literally the direction to fly.
The answer needs both sources, because the words name the behavior and the diagram explains the code that makes 'points the way' make sense.

items.prompt:
Passage: A sports writer claimed that interest in town softball is 'fading fast' and that 'fewer teams sign up every year.' She argued the league might close soon. The league office disagreed and shared its own records. The passage repeats the writer's claim that team numbers fall 'every year' without exception.

Table 1: Number of softball teams that registered each season
Season 2018: 12 teams
Season 2019: 14 teams
Season 2020: 11 teams
Season 2021: 13 teams
Season 2022: 15 teams

Using both the passage and Table 1, explain how the table complicates the writer's claim that fewer teams sign up 'every year.'
items.answer: The table complicates the claim because the number of teams does not fall every year. It rose from 12 to 14 (2018 to 2019), rose from 11 to 13 (2020 to 2021), and rose again from 13 to 15 (2021 to 2022). Since teams increased in several years, the table contradicts the writer's words that fewer teams sign up every single year.

steps: The words make an absolute claim: fewer teams 'every year' with no exceptions.
The table gives the year by year counts the writer did not show, so I check whether they always drop.
Track the changes: 12 up to 14, down to 11, up to 13, up to 15. Several years go up, not down.
Because the data rises in multiple years, the format contradicts rather than confirms the words.
Combine the sources: the writer's 'every year' claim is too strong, and the table is needed to expose that the trend is mixed, not a steady fall.

items.prompt:
Passage: The town of Cedar Falls grew quickly after a paper mill opened. Older residents recall that 'the population doubled in just a few years' once mill jobs appeared, though the passage never lists the exact figures. Local historians say the boom faded after the mill cut back its workforce. The passage describes a sharp rise followed by a slower decline but provides no numbers.

Table 1: Population of Cedar Falls by year
Year 1950: 2,000 people
Year 1955: 4,100 people
Year 1960: 4,300 people
Year 1965: 3,900 people
Year 1970: 3,600 people

Using both the passage and Table 1, which two years best show the 'population doubled in just a few years,' and how do you know?
items.answer: The years 1950 and 1955 best show the doubling. The table shows the population rose from 2,000 in 1950 to 4,100 in 1955, which is just over double in five years. This matches the passage's claim that the population 'doubled in just a few years' after the mill opened.

steps: The words claim the population 'doubled in just a few years' but give no figures, so the table must supply them.
Doubling means the number roughly twice as large, so I look for a pair of close years where the count about doubles.
Compare 1950 (2,000) and 1955 (4,100): 4,100 is just over twice 2,000, and the years are only five apart.
Other pairs do not double: 1955 to 1960 barely changes, and the later years fall.
Combine: the table's 1950 and 1955 figures give the concrete evidence for the passage's claim about doubling, so neither source alone is enough.

items.prompt:
Passage: Sea turtles return to the same beaches to lay their eggs. Conservation workers in one country counted nests for several seasons. A news article reported that protection efforts were 'finally paying off' and that nests were 'on the rise.' The article did not say in which season the recovery began. Workers say the first clear jump in nests marks the turning point.

Chart 1: Number of sea turtle nests counted each season
Season 2015: 220 nests
Season 2016: 210 nests
Season 2017: 215 nests
Season 2018: 340 nests
Season 2019: 480 nests

Using both the passage and Chart 1, which season marks the start of the recovery the article describes, and how do you know?
items.answer: Season 2018 marks the start of the recovery. The chart shows nests stayed near 210 to 220 in 2015 through 2017, then jumped to 340 in 2018 and kept rising to 480 in 2019. This first clear jump in 2018 matches the article's claim that nests were 'finally' on the rise.

steps: The words say efforts were 'finally paying off' and nests were 'on the rise' but do not name the season.
The chart provides the season by season counts the words leave out.
Find where the numbers stop holding flat and clearly increase: 2015 to 2017 stay near 210 to 220, then 2018 jumps to 340.
The word 'finally' signals a turning point, which the data shows at the first big rise in 2018.
Combine: the article describes a recovery and the chart pinpoints 2018 as where it begins, so both sources are needed.

items.prompt:
Passage: Explorers in the 1800s searched for a water route across a northern region. One team's journal says they 'left the trading post, crossed the wide river, climbed past the tall falls, and finally reached the cold lake where supplies ran out.' The journal lists places in the order the team passed them but gives no directions or distances.

Map 1: Labeled landmarks from west to east
Trading Post is on the far west.
Wide River is just east of the Trading Post.
Tall Falls is east of the Wide River.
Cold Lake is on the far east.

Using both the passage and Map 1, in which overall direction did the team travel, and how do you know?
items.answer: The team traveled from west to east. The journal lists the places in this order: Trading Post, Wide River, Tall Falls, Cold Lake. The map shows those same landmarks running from the far west (Trading Post) to the far east (Cold Lake), so following the journal's order means moving eastward.

steps: The words give the order of places but no compass direction, so direction must come from the map.
List the journal order: Trading Post, then Wide River, then Tall Falls, then Cold Lake.
Read the map's layout: those same landmarks are placed from far west to far east in that exact order.
Match the order of travel to the map's positions: each next stop is farther east than the last.
Combine: the journal supplies the sequence and the map supplies the directions, so together they show the team moved west to east.

items.prompt:
Passage: A science museum claims its new energy exhibit is its 'most visited ever.' A reporter wanted to check whether the exhibit truly drew the largest crowds. The museum said attendance 'set a record in its opening month.' The passage repeats the museum's claim but offers no attendance figures of its own.

Table 1: Visitors in the opening month of recent exhibits
Dinosaur Hall: 9,400 visitors
Space Gallery: 11,200 visitors
Ocean World: 8,700 visitors
Energy Exhibit: 10,800 visitors
Weather Lab: 7,500 visitors

Using both the passage and Table 1, does the data fully support the museum's claim that the Energy Exhibit was its 'most visited ever'? Explain.
items.answer: No, the data does not fully support the claim. The table shows the Energy Exhibit drew 10,800 visitors in its opening month, but the Space Gallery drew more, with 11,200 visitors. Since another exhibit had higher attendance, the table contradicts the museum's claim that the Energy Exhibit was the 'most visited ever.'

steps: The words claim the Energy Exhibit was the 'most visited ever,' but give no numbers to prove it.
The table supplies the visitor counts needed to test the claim.
Find the Energy Exhibit's count: 10,800 visitors.
Compare it to the others: Space Gallery has 11,200, which is higher than 10,800.
Combine: because the data shows a different exhibit drew more visitors, the table contradicts the museum's words, so the claim is not fully supported.

items.prompt:
Passage: A history class studied how a town's railroad station changed over time. Their teacher said the station was 'rebuilt twice and finally closed' but did not give the years. The class found a record of key dates. They learned that the closing happened many years after the second rebuild, leaving the building empty for decades.

Timeline 1: Key dates for the railroad station
Year 1880: Station first built
Year 1905: Station rebuilt after a fire
Year 1930: Station rebuilt again, larger
Year 1972: Station closed to passengers
Year 1995: Building turned into a museum

Using both the passage and Timeline 1, in what year did the second rebuild happen, and how many years passed before the station closed?
items.answer: The second rebuild happened in 1930. The station closed in 1972, so 42 years passed between the second rebuild and the closing (1972 minus 1930). The timeline supplies the years the teacher's words left out.

steps: The words say the station was 'rebuilt twice and finally closed' but give no years.
The timeline lists the dates, so I read it to find the rebuilds and the closing.
The two rebuilds are 1905 (after a fire) and 1930 (larger), so the second rebuild is 1930.
The closing date is 1972.
Subtract to find the gap: 1972 minus 1930 equals 42 years. Combining the words' sequence with the timeline's dates gives the full answer.

items.prompt:
Passage: A city report says recycling has 'grown enormously' since the city placed bins on every street. Officials credited the bins for the increase and predicted that recycling would keep climbing. The report describes the rise as steady and large but, oddly, never states the actual tons collected. Critics asked for the numbers before believing the praise.

Chart 1: Tons of material recycled each year
Year 2017: 1,200 tons
Year 2018: 1,650 tons
Year 2019: 2,100 tons
Year 2020: 2,900 tons
Year 2021: 3,500 tons

Using both the passage and Chart 1, how many more tons were recycled in 2021 than in 2017, and how does that figure support the report's words 'grown enormously'?
items.answer: In 2021 the city recycled 2,300 more tons than in 2017 (3,500 minus 1,200). This nearly threefold increase supports the report's phrase 'grown enormously,' because the chart provides the large, concrete rise that the words only described in general terms.

steps: The words say recycling 'grown enormously' but provide no tonnage, so the chart must supply the figures.
Find the 2017 amount: 1,200 tons.
Find the 2021 amount: 3,500 tons.
Subtract to find the increase: 3,500 minus 1,200 equals 2,300 tons, almost triple the start.
Combine: the chart's large gain backs up the words 'grown enormously,' and neither the vague words nor a single number alone tells the full story.

items.prompt:
Passage: A nature guide explains that a certain owl is 'most active right after sunset.' Birdwatchers wanted to know the best hour to spot it. The guide adds that the owl hunts in the dark and rests during the day, but it never names a specific time to watch. Researchers recorded how often the owl was seen each hour one evening.

Table 1: Owl sightings by hour one evening
6 p.m.: 2 sightings
7 p.m.: 5 sightings
8 p.m.: 14 sightings
9 p.m.: 9 sightings
10 p.m.: 4 sightings

The sun set at about 7:45 p.m. that evening. Using both the passage and Table 1, which hour best matches the guide's claim that the owl is 'most active right after sunset'? Explain.
items.answer: The 8 p.m. hour best matches the claim. The sun set near 7:45 p.m., so 8 p.m. is right after sunset, and the table shows the most sightings then, with 14. This combines the guide's claim about timing with the data's peak to identify the best hour to watch.

steps: The words say the owl is 'most active right after sunset' but do not give a clock hour.
Two pieces of given information matter: sunset was about 7:45 p.m., and the table counts sightings by hour.
Find the peak in the table: 8 p.m. has 14 sightings, the highest of any hour.
Check that 8 p.m. is 'right after sunset': since sunset was 7:45 p.m., the 8 p.m. hour follows it closely.
Combine: the words point to just after sunset, and the data's peak at 8 p.m. matches that window, so 8 p.m. is the answer.

items.prompt:
Passage: A travel article praises a mountain village as 'cool all summer,' calling it a perfect escape from the heat. It says visitors can leave a hot lowland city and enjoy gentle weather in the hills. The article repeats that the village stays 'cool all summer' but gives no temperatures, so a reader cannot tell how cool it really is.

Table 1: Average July high temperatures
Lowland City: 36 degrees Celsius
Mountain Village: 24 degrees Celsius
Coastal Town: 29 degrees Celsius
Desert Outpost: 41 degrees Celsius
Forest Camp: 26 degrees Celsius

Using both the passage and Table 1, how many degrees cooler is the Mountain Village than the Lowland City in July, and how does this support the article's claim?
items.answer: The Mountain Village is 12 degrees Celsius cooler than the Lowland City in July (36 minus 24). This sizable difference supports the article's claim that the village is 'cool all summer' and a good escape from the heat, because the table provides the temperatures the words left out.

steps: The words call the village 'cool all summer' but give no temperatures, so the table must supply them.
Find the Mountain Village July high: 24 degrees Celsius.
Find the Lowland City July high: 36 degrees Celsius.
Subtract to find the difference: 36 minus 24 equals 12 degrees Celsius cooler.
Combine: the 12 degree gap gives concrete backing to the words 'cool all summer' and shows why the village is an escape from the city's heat.

items.prompt:
Passage: A report on a national park says visitors 'crowd the trails in spring' and that crowds 'thin out by fall.' The park hopes to spread visits more evenly across the year. The report describes spring as the busiest season and fall as quieter but gives no visitor counts. A ranger said the busiest month is not the same as the busiest season.

Chart 1: Visitors per month at the park
March: 18,000 visitors
April: 25,000 visitors
May: 31,000 visitors
July: 22,000 visitors
October: 12,000 visitors

Using both the passage and Chart 1, which month had the most visitors, and does the data support the report's claim that spring is the busiest time?
items.answer: May had the most visitors, with 31,000. Since March, April, and May are spring months and they show high counts (peaking at 31,000 in May) while October has only 12,000, the data supports the report's claim that spring is the busiest time and crowds thin out by fall.

steps: The words claim spring is busiest and fall is quieter but give no numbers.
The chart supplies monthly visitor counts to test the claim.
Find the highest month: May at 31,000 is the largest of all listed months.
Check the seasons: the spring months (March, April, May) climb to that 31,000 peak, while October (fall) is lowest at 12,000.
Combine: the chart confirms the words, since the busiest month (May) and the high spring totals match 'crowd the trails in spring,' and the low October number matches 'thin out by fall.'

items.prompt:
Passage: A school newspaper reported that the chess club is 'the fastest growing club at our school.' The writer urged students to join before meetings filled up. The article said membership 'shot up this year' compared with last year but printed no actual member counts for any club, so readers could not check which club grew fastest.

Table 1: Club membership, last year and this year
Chess Club: last year 10, this year 28
Drama Club: last year 30, this year 45
Coding Club: last year 12, this year 20
Art Club: last year 25, this year 33
Debate Club: last year 8, this year 14

Using both the passage and Table 1, does the data support the claim that the Chess Club is the 'fastest growing' club? Explain using the change in members.
items.answer: Yes, the data supports the claim. The Chess Club grew by 18 members (from 10 to 28), which is the largest increase of any club listed. The Drama Club grew by 15, Coding by 8, Art by 8, and Debate by 6, so the Chess Club's gain of 18 is the biggest. This matches the article's words that membership 'shot up this year.'

steps: The words claim the Chess Club is 'fastest growing' but give no member numbers, so the table must supply them.

Compute each club's change by subtracting last year from this year: Chess 28 minus 10 equals 18; Drama 45 minus 30 equals 15; Coding 20 minus 12 equals 8; Art 33 minus 25 equals 8; Debate 14 minus 8 equals 6.
Compare the increases: 18 is larger than 15, 8, 8, and 6.
Because the Chess Club's gain of 18 is the biggest, it grew the most.
Combine: the table's growth figures confirm the article's claim, and neither the words alone nor a single membership number alone would prove which club grew fastest.
